name: Software engineering: pairwise covering array for the Apache configuration model
description: Build a smallest pairwise covering array for the 172-option Apache web-server model of Cohen et al., avoiding its forbidden option combinations. Every feasible pair of option settings must appear in some test configuration; fewer configurations is better.

sources.locator: Cohen, Dwyer and Shi (TSE 2008): constrained interaction testing of highly configurable systems; introduces the SPIN, GCC, Apache and Bugzilla constraint models and a SAT-checked greedy construction.
Jia, Cohen, Harman and Petke (ICSE 2015): hyperheuristic search for constrained covering arrays; publishes the benchmark archive used here.
ICSE15_HHSA_Benchmarks.zip (CC BY 4.0): CASA-format model and constraint files; levels are numbered from 1.
Supplementary table of the FastCA repository: HHSA and CASA sizes (2-way and 3-way, 5-hour cutoff) on the same HHSA-format instance files.

limitations: Published sizes on these exact files: HHSA 30 rows and CASA 32 rows (FastCA repository supplementary table, minimum over runs with a 5-hour cutoff).
The array size is the only objective; generation time is bounded by the sandbox CPU limit and is not scored, whereas the published solvers ran for 1000 s to 5 h in C++.
Feasible combinations are decided by an exact search at preparation time and cross-checked with Z3 in the tests; a Z3 disagreement would change the required set.
The models are public; a candidate could embed a precomputed array. Scores are comparable with published sizes only for arrays generated within the contract.

requirements.datasets: One CASA model from the ICSE 2015 CIT benchmark archive (Zenodo 581657, CC BY 4.0), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: HHSA reports a 30-row pairwise array on this model (FastCA repository supplementary table). No valid array can have fewer rows: the 6-level and 5-level options have 30 feasible level pairs, which must occur in distinct rows (counting bound recomputed here). The published array itself was not re-checked here. The value therefore equals the counting lower bound: it is the optimum, so this instance cannot show a new state of the art.

name: Software engineering: test-based repair of the QuixBugs Python programs
description: Write a general repair procedure that receives a buggy QuixBugs Python program with a few visible tests and returns a patch of at most two statements. A patch counts only when it also passes held-out QuixBugs tests and generated tests whose expected outputs come from the reference fix.

sources.locator: Lin, Koppel, Chen and Solar-Lezama (SPLASH Companion 2017): the QuixBugs benchmark of 40 programs with one-line bugs in Python and Java.
Pinned QuixBugs commit (MIT licence): python_programs, correct_python_programs (used only at preparation time) and json_testcases.
Le Goues, Nguyen, Forrest and Weimer (TSE 2012): GenProg, test-suite-based generate-and-validate repair.
Smith, Barr, Le Goues and Brun (ESEC/FSE 2015): patches that pass the repair tests but fail held-out tests (overfitting).
Ye, Martinez, Durieux and Monperrus (JSS 2021): repair tools on QuixBugs; plausible patches checked for overfitting with generated tests.

limitations: Uses the 31 Python programs with JSON tests; the nine graph programs are excluded, so results reported on all 40 programs are not comparable, nor are results of tools that call language models.

Correctness is decided by tests: the visible tests, the remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated inputs per program checked against the reference fix. A semantically different but test-equivalent patch counts as a repair, and a wrong patch that agrees on all these inputs would also count; there is no manual patch review.
Generated inputs respect the documented preconditions and avoid inputs whose correct output is not unique; inputs on which the reference fix itself loops (some wrap cases) are excluded.
The programs and their fixes are public, so a candidate could embed remembered fixes; the contract excludes this but it cannot be checked automatically.
Each repair() call gets 4 s of CPU time in a Python sandbox, far less than the hours given to repair tools in the literature.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.

requirements.datasets: QuixBugs at commit 4257f44b (MIT), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py; the reference fixes are used only to derive held-out tests and are not stored.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published result uses this 31-program subset with these held-out tests. Ye et al. (2021) report repair tools on all 40 Java QuixBugs programs, and language-model studies report counts on all 40 Python programs under other correctness criteria.

sources.title: A comprehensive study of automatic program repair on the QuixBugs benchmark

name: Software engineering: optimal register coalescing on the challenge graphs with fewer than 3,000 nodes
description: Colour the 452 smaller interference graphs of the Appel-George Optimal Coalescing Challenge with 6 registers so that as much move (affinity) weight as possible joins nodes of the same colour. The score is the mean share of affinity weight left uncoalesced; lower is better.

sources.locator: Appel and George, Optimal Coalescing Challenge (2000): 474 interference graphs with affinities, problem and solution format, checker and published solution sets.
Appel and George (PLDI 2001): optimal spilling by integer programming followed by coalescing; source of the challenge graphs.
George and Appel (TOPLAS 1996): iterated register coalescing, the heuristic behind the published greedy solution set.
Grund and Hack (CC 2007): cutting-plane ILP for optimal coalescing; their solutions of all 474 challenge instances are on the challenge page.
Park and Moon (TOPLAS 2004): optimistic register coalescing, the basis of the published optimistic solution set.

limitations: All 452 best-known costs are the published Grund-Hack ILP solutions, which CPLEX reported optimal; this evaluator recomputed their costs exactly but did not re-prove optimality.
The score averages per-instance shares of uncoalesced affinity weight; the challenge itself evaluates instances separately, so totals in the literature are not the same number.
All graphs come from one compiler (SML/NJ) with six registers after optimal spilling; methods tuned on them may not transfer to other register files or allocators.
The instances are public; a candidate could embed precomputed colourings, which the contract excludes.
The candidate gets 120 s of CPU time in total in a Python sandbox; published solvers had no comparable limit.

requirements.datasets: Optimal Coalescing Challenge graphs and the published Grund-Hack, iterated-coalescing and optimistic solution sets (no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URLs and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: Mean uncoalesced share of the Grund-Hack ILP solutions, reported optimal by CPLEX for every instance in this group and recomputed here. The published iterated-register-coalescing and optimistic-coalescing solution sets score 0.0230 and 0.0148.

name: Software engineering: history-based test prioritisation in continuous integration (ABB Paint Control)
description: Order the test cases of each of the 352 continuous-integration cycles of ABB's Paint Control system so that failing tests run early, using only the verdicts of earlier cycles. Each cycle's verdicts are revealed after its order is committed; the score is the mean APFD over cycles with both failing and passing tests.

sources.locator: Spieker, Gotlieb, Marijan and Mossige (ISSTA 2017): reinforcement learning for test prioritisation and selection in CI; introduces the ABB Paint Control and IOF/ROL data.
Pinned atcs-data commit (MIT licence): paintcontrol.csv and iofrol.csv with cycle, test, duration and verdict columns.
Elbaum, Rothermel and Penix (FSE 2014): history-based test prioritisation and selection in continuous integration at Google.
Rothermel, Untch, Chu and Harrold (TSE 2001): test case prioritisation and the APFD metric.

limitations: The verdicts are historical: the order cannot change which tests fail, and every test of a cycle is assumed to run.

Plain APFD with each failing test counted as one fault; the source paper reports NAPFD under a time budget, so its numbers are not directly comparable. Durations are given to the candidate but not used by the metric.
Repeated executions of a test within one cycle are merged (failed if any execution failed); the data set's LastRun and LastResults columns and its row order are not passed on.
Ordering failing tests first gives 0.903 on this data; a last-verdict heuristic (the seed) gives 0.742.
The verdicts are public; embedding them is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.

requirements.datasets: ABB Paint Control CI history from HelgeS/atcs-data at commit 85bae8b6 (MIT), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: Published results on this data use NAPFD under a time budget or other aggregations, so no directly comparable value is embedded; the best possible score for this metric (failing tests first) is reported in the evaluator details.

name: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's tomllib
description: Generate at most 1,000 input strings that drive the TOML parser tomllib (CPython 3.12.14) through as many code blocks as possible. The score is the number of distinct instrumented blocks (function entries, branch outcomes, loop exits, handlers) that the inputs reach.

sources.locator: Bohme, Pham and Roychoudhury (CCS 2016): coverage-based greybox fuzzing, where reaching new coverage guides input generation.
Godefroid, Kiezun and Levin (PLDI 2008): grammar-based fuzzing of parsers to reach code beyond the lexer.
Klees, Ruef, Cooper, Wei and Hicks (CCS 2018): how fuzzers are evaluated, including coverage as a measure.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the pure-Python target modules and the test inputs used as references.

limitations: Coverage is a proxy: no faults are seeded and crashes are not scored, while fuzzing research also measures bugs found (Klees et al. 2018).
Block probes are this evaluator's own instrumentation of the pinned sources (no coverage.py or compiler edges), so counts are not comparable with other coverage tools; some probes are unreachable.
The corpus is bounded by size (1,000 strings of at most 2,000 characters) and generation by 60 s of CPU time instead of the hours-long wall-clock budgets of fuzzing benchmarks.
Reference computed here: the 62 TOML files of CPython's tomllib test data reach 278 of the 305 probes; the random-string seed reaches fewer.
The target is pure Python executed by CPython; results say nothing about memory-safety bugs in C code.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this instrumentation. As a reference, the 62 TOML files of CPython's tomllib test data reach 278 of the 305 probes (computed with this evaluator).

name: Software engineering: mutation-adequate test generation for CPython's textwrap
description: Generate at most 30 test calls for textwrap (wrap, fill, shorten, dedent, indent) that distinguish as many of its 132 first-order mutants as possible from the original module. A mutant is killed when some test's result or exception type differs; the score is the fraction killed.

sources.locator: Fraser and Zeller (TSE 2012): generating unit tests and oracles that kill mutants.
DeMillo and Offutt (TSE 1991): constraint-based generation of test data that kills mutants.
Lukasczyk, Kroiss and Fraser (EMSE 2023): automated unit test generation for Python (Pynguin), assessed by coverage and mutation score.
Papadakis, Jia, Harman and Le Traon (ICSE 2015): trivial compiler equivalence for removing equivalent mutants.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the mutated modules.

limitations: Mutants come from this evaluator's operator set (MutPy- and mutmut-style replacements inside function bodies); scores are not comparable with other mutation tools.
Non-compiling, duplicate and trivially compiler-equivalent mutants are removed, but other equivalent mutants remain, so 1.0 is unreachable and the number of killable mutants is unknown.
Oracles are regression oracles: a test kills a mutant when the hash of the result's repr or the exception type differs from the original's, which also counts differences a specification might allow.

Reference computed with this evaluator (Linux x86-64, CPython 3.12): the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000, i.e. 2,000 random calls, kills 100 of the 132 mutants (75.8%); the 30-test budget is this dataset's choice.
The candidate sees the mutants and may run them, so the task measures test generation and selection against known mutants, not generalisation to unseen faults.

Step counting makes the verdict on loops independent of the machine, but CPU-time limits remain as a safety net: a test whose call on the original module needs about 0.2 s of CPU time (very large powers, tab expansion to megabytes or long exact-fraction computations: 9,999 quantiles of 40 fractions need 0.06 s on the machine used for this record) is used or ignored depending on the machine.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this mutant set. As a reference, the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000 (2,000 random calls) kills 100 of the 132 mutants (75.8%) (computed with this evaluator on Linux x86-64).

sources.title: Mutation-Driven Generation of Unit Tests and Oracles

Step counting makes the verdict on loops independent of the machine, but CPU-time limits remain as a safety net: a test whose call on the original module needs about 0.2 s of CPU time (very large powers, tab expansion to megabytes or long exact-fraction computations: 9,999 quantiles of 40 fractions need 0.06 s on the machine used for this record) is used or ignored depending on the machine.

name: Software engineering: loop-invariant inference for the Code2Inv programs
description: Infer a loop invariant for each of the 124 valid Code2Inv C programs so that Z3 proves initiation, consecution and the post-condition. The procedure may query a verifier that returns counterexamples (50 queries per program); the score is the fraction of programs with a proven invariant.

sources.locator: Si, Dai, Raghothaman, Naik and Song (NeurIPS 2018): Code2Inv, learning loop invariants with a verifier in the loop; introduces the 133-program benchmark.
Pinned Code2Inv benchmark directory: C programs (C_instances/c) and SMT-LIB verification conditions (C_instances/c_smt2); no licence stated.
Ryan, Wong, Yao, Gu and Jana (ICLR 2020): CLN2INV; removes 9 invalid programs and solves all 124 others (LoopInvGen 104, Code2Inv 90), one hour per problem.
Garg, Loding, Madhusudan and Neider (CAV 2014): ICE learning, invariant inference from a teacher's implication and counterexamples.
Flanagan and Leino (FME 2001): Houdini, the template-based invariant pruning used by the seed.

limitations: Of the 133 programs, bounded model checking here finds 9 whose post-condition can fail (26, 27, 31, 32, 61, 62, 72, 75, 106), the count reported by Ryan et al. (2020); those 9 are excluded, so scores use 124 programs.
Five of the 124 post-conditions hold at every loop exit, so the invariant 'true' already proves them; many others need only simple bounds.

Correctness follows the benchmark's own SMT-LIB verification conditions, checked by Z3 with a fixed resource limit; the C programs themselves are not executed, so an error in an encoding would carry over.

Invariants are restricted to linear integer arithmetic and the candidate has 50 verifier queries per program and 180 s of CPU in total, while published tools had one hour per program and unbounded solver calls (LoopInvGen averaged about 3,600 calls); published counts are therefore not directly comparable.
The programs are public and solved invariants circulate; embedding them is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically.
Results depend on the Z3 version only where a check reaches the resource limit; this run used z3-solver 5.1.0.

requirements.datasets: Code2Inv C programs and verification conditions (PL-ML/code2inv at commit 336a7063, no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URL and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: CLN2INV proves all 124 valid programs (LoopInvGen 104, Code2Inv 90) with one hour per program and unbounded solver calls (Ryan et al. 2020, Table 1); their invariants were not re-checked with this evaluator. The score is the fraction of programs proven, so 1.0 is its maximum: the optimum is attained and this instance cannot show a new state of the art.

name: Software engineering: superoptimisation of the 25 Hacker's Delight kernels
description: Rewrite each of 25 bit-manipulation kernels (Hacker's Delight, as used by Brahma and STOKE) into the shortest straight-line program over 32-bit operations that Z3 proves equal to the reference for every input. The score is the total instruction count; unproven programs count at the reference length.

sources.locator: Massalin (ASPLOS 1987): the superoptimizer, an exhaustive search for the shortest instruction sequence computing a function.
Gulwani, Jha, Tiwari and Venkatesan (PLDI 2011): synthesis of loop-free programs; defines the 25 Hacker's Delight benchmarks P1-P25.
Schkufza, Sharma and Aiken (ASPLOS 2013): stochastic superoptimization (STOKE), evaluated on the same 25 kernels.
STOKE's straight-line C versions of p01-p25 (Apache-2.0); the reference programs are parsed from these files, with p12, p13, p20 and p24 corrected.
Phothilimthana, Thakur, Bodik and Dhurjati (ASPLOS 2016): scaling up superoptimization with an enumerative and stochastic search.

limitations: The 32-bit instruction set with unit costs is this dataset's choice; STOKE optimises x86-64 code for latency and Brahma synthesises from given component multisets, so published program sizes are not directly comparable.

STOKE's C files for p12, p13, p20 and p24 compute other functions than the named kernels (operand swap, signed instead of unsigned shift or division, and a wrong final operand); these four were corrected, and all 25 references were checked against independent Python specifications and against the clang-compiled corrected C on 100,000 inputs.
C's undefined cases (division by zero in p20 at x = 0, shifts by 32 or more in p19) follow SMT-LIB semantics, so equivalence is required on those inputs too.

A program counts only if Z3 proves equivalence within a fixed resource limit; a correct program whose proof exceeds the limit counts at the reference length. Proofs for all programs tried here took well under a second.

The reference total is 135 instructions; minimal lengths in this instruction set are unknown. Shorter verified programs exist (for example 3 instead of 10 instructions for the power-of-two test), so the reference is not the state of the art.
The kernels are public and textbook solutions are well known; returning remembered programs is allowed by the score but the contract asks for a search procedure.

requirements.datasets: STOKE examples/hacker p01-p25 C files (Apache-2.0, commit 98d8a0f0), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published total exists for this instruction set; the reference programs total 135 instructions and are not minimal.

name: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
description: Rank the code blocks of a faulty module by suspiciousness using only its program spectrum: for each block, how many failing and passing tests execute it. The 532 faults are first-order mutants of textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions; the score is the mean EXAM (rank of the faulty block divided by the number of blocks).

sources.locator: Jones and Harrold (ASE 2005): the Tarantula fault-localisation technique and its evaluation by the share of code examined (the seed).
Abreu, Zoeteweij and van Gemund (TAIC PART 2007): accuracy of spectrum-based fault localisation with block hit spectra; Ochiai coefficient.
Wong, Debroy, Gao and Li (IEEE Trans. Reliability 2014): the DStar formula.
Yoo (SSBSE 2012): evolving risk-evaluation formulas with genetic programming, the program-search setting of this task.
Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017): results on artificial faults do not carry over to real faults; the main caveat of this task.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions.

limitations: Faults are artificial first-order mutants, one per version; Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017) found that rankings of fault-localisation techniques on artificial faults do not predict their rankings on real faults.

Spectra are block hit counts from this evaluator's probes and a seeded 240-call test pool per module, not statement coverage of a project's own test suite; the faulty block is the statement-level block containing the mutated statement (faults on one-line compound statements are left out), so EXAM values are not comparable with published ones.
Undetected mutants and mutants that break the import are excluded; textwrap contributes 110 faults, urllib.parse 183 and fractions 239.

Reference values computed here: Tarantula (the seed) 0.0506, Ochiai 0.0268 and DStar(2) 0.0248 mean EXAM; ranking each faulty block first among blocks with an identical spectrum would give 0.0087, a bound for formulas of the counts that no single formula need reach.

Blocks and faults are shown in a random order that changes with every evaluation, so neither a position nor the number of the call carries information; the score of a formula of the counts does not depend on the order. The faults are public, however: a spectrum identifies its fault, and a search can still overfit this fault set.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence); spectra derived by scripts/prepare_software.py with the evaluator's mutants and test pools.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for these faults. Computed with this evaluator: Tarantula 0.0506, Ochiai 0.0268 and DStar(2) 0.0248 mean EXAM.

sources.title: The DStar Method for Effective Software Fault Localization

name: Software engineering: log parsing (event template identification) on the 16 Loghub-2k data sets
description: Group the messages of 16 system logs (2,000 lines each, from HDFS, Hadoop, Spark, Linux, OpenSSH and others) by the log statement that produced them, given only the message texts. The score is the mean grouping accuracy against the corrected ground-truth events.

sources.locator: He, Zhu, Zheng and Lyu (ICWS 2017): Drain, online log parsing with a fixed-depth tree; the reference parser.
Makanju, Zincir-Heywood and Milios (KDD 2009): IPLoM, clustering event logs by iterative partitioning.
Zhu et al. (ICSE-SEIP 2019): the Loghub-2k benchmark (16 systems x 2,000 lines) and the grouping-accuracy metric.
Khan, Shin, Bianculli and Briand (ICSE 2022): corrected Loghub-2k ground truth, used here.
Pinned logparser repository: data/loghub_2k_corrected (Loghub licence, research or academic use with attribution) and the Drain implementation and evaluator used for the reference check.

limitations: Grouping accuracy is the classic metric; later work also reports parsing accuracy of the template strings and template-level F1 (Jiang et al., ISSTA 2024), which are not scored here.
Each data set has only 2,000 messages, and newer, larger annotations (Loghub-2.0) show lower accuracies for the same parsers; results here say little about scale.

The candidate gets message contents with the headers already removed by the benchmark's log formats, so header parsing is not part of the task; per-data-set settings, as in the published benchmarks, are allowed.

Reference values computed with this evaluator: logparser's Drain with its benchmark settings scores 0.8605 mean grouping accuracy on the corrected labels (0.8654 on the original labels, as published); the digit-masking seed scores 0.7937.
The logs and their labels are public; embedding labels is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically. The Loghub licence permits research or academic use with attribution only.

requirements.datasets: Loghub-2k with corrected labels from logpai/logparser at commit d9d41807 (Loghub licence: research or academic use with attribution; not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: No directly comparable published value exists for the corrected labels. As a reference computed with this evaluator, logparser's Drain (He et al. 2017) with its published benchmark settings scores 0.8605 mean grouping accuracy on these labels; on the original Loghub-2k labels it scores 0.8654, reproducing the published table exactly. Language-model-based parsers report higher accuracies but are outside this CPU contract.

name: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's plistlib (XML and binary property lists)
description: Generate at most 1,000 inputs (each a string whose characters are bytes) that drive plistlib.loads (CPython 3.12.14), which detects and parses XML and binary property lists, through as many code blocks as possible. The score is the number of distinct instrumented blocks the inputs reach.

sources.locator: Bohme, Pham and Roychoudhury (CCS 2016): coverage-based greybox fuzzing, where reaching new coverage guides input generation.
Godefroid, Kiezun and Levin (PLDI 2008): grammar-based fuzzing of parsers to reach code beyond the lexer.
Klees, Ruef, Cooper, Wei and Hicks (CCS 2018): how fuzzers are evaluated, including coverage as a measure.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the pure-Python target modules and the test inputs used as references.

limitations: Coverage is a proxy: no faults are seeded and crashes are not scored, while fuzzing research also measures bugs found (Klees et al. 2018).
Block probes are this evaluator's own instrumentation of the pinned sources (no coverage.py or compiler edges), so counts are not comparable with other coverage tools; some probes are unreachable.
The corpus is bounded by size (1,000 strings of at most 2,000 characters) and generation by 60 s of CPU time instead of the hours-long wall-clock budgets of fuzzing benchmarks.

Reference computed here: the 58 byte strings embedded in CPython's test_plistlib.py (XML and binary samples, some longer than the 2,000-character limit) reach 111 of the 317 probes; random printable strings (the seed) reach 15.

The probes cover the whole module, including the plist writers that loads never calls, so the reachable maximum is well below 317; the XML path also runs the C expat parser, whose coverage is not counted.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this instrumentation. As a reference, the 58 byte strings embedded in CPython's test_plistlib.py reach 111 of the 317 probes (computed with this evaluator).

description: Generate at most 30 test calls for statistics (averages, medians, quantiles, spread, correlation, regression and NormalDist) that distinguish as many of its 583 first-order mutants as possible from the original module. A mutant is killed when some test's result or exception type differs; the score is the fraction killed.

DeMillo and Offutt (TSE 1991): constraint-based generation of test data that kills mutants.

Reference computed with this evaluator (Linux x86-64, CPython 3.12): the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000, i.e. 2,000 random calls, kills 345 of the 583 mutants (59.2%); the 30-test budget is this dataset's choice.
The candidate sees the mutants and may run them, so the task measures test generation and selection against known mutants, not generalisation to unseen faults.
The module's optional C accelerator for NormalDist.inv_cdf (_statistics) is disabled by a one-line patch so that its Python implementation is the one mutated and tested.

name: Software engineering: programming by example for string transformations (SyGuS-Comp PBE strings)
description: Write a synthesiser that, from a few input-output examples and a grammar, returns a string-manipulation program (phone numbers, names, initials, university addresses) that also reproduces held-out examples of the same task. The score is the fraction of 27 SyGuS-Comp tasks solved.

sources.locator: Gulwani (POPL 2011): FlashFill, synthesising string transformations in spreadsheets from input-output examples.
Alur et al. (FMCAD 2013): syntax-guided synthesis, the problem format (grammar plus specification) of these tasks.
Alur, Radhakrishna and Udupa (TACAS 2017): EUSolver, enumerative synthesis with divide and conquer, evaluated on SyGuS PBE string tasks.
Padhi, Millstein, Nori and Sharma (CAV 2019): overfitting in synthesis, programs that fit the examples but not the intended function.
Pinned SyGuS benchmarks (no licence stated): the base and '-long' files of the 27 tasks.

limitations: Only 27 tasks, from a few families (11 phone-number tasks, 4 name-combination tasks, 6 university-address tasks and 6 others), so scores move in steps of 1/27 and families are correlated.

Correctness is judged on examples: the given ones plus 8 to 94 held-out examples of the '-long' variant per task (3 to 94 distinct ones, because the long files repeat examples; bikes has 3); a program that agrees on all of them but differs elsewhere counts as solved.

SyGuS-Comp scored consistency with the given examples and solving time, not generalisation, so published solved counts are not comparable; the benchmark repository notes that errors and duplicates may exist.
The bottom-up enumeration seed solves 8 of 27 within its budget; the tasks are public and solutions could be remembered, which the contract excludes but cannot check.

The interpreter implements the SMT-LIB 2.6 string semantics used by SyGuS-Comp 2018 and was cross-checked against Z3 on random terms; a solver with different edge-case semantics could disagree on unusual programs.

requirements.datasets: SyGuS-Org/benchmarks PBE_SLIA_Track/from_2018 at commit 13c8deb6 (no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URL and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value measures generalisation to the held-out '-long' examples of these 27 tasks; the bottom-up enumeration seed solves 8 (computed here).
